name: Aga Khan University boosts training on Antimicrobial Resistance

content.title: Aga Khan University boosts training on Antimicrobial Resistance
content.summary: The conference aims to fill critical gaps in the surveillance of antimicrobial-resistant bacteria in low- and middle-income countries

media.caption: Dr Emmanuel Tanui, Ministry of Health AMR Focal Point (L), Prof Gunturu Revathi, Section Head of Clinical Microbiology, AKU Medical College, East Africa, (M) Dr Kamran Hameed, Chair, Department of Medicine, AKU Dar es Salaam Campus.
media.alt: Aga Khan University boosts training on Antimicrobial Resistance

content.text: The 2024 Microbiology Updates Conference organised by the Aga Khan University (AKU) Medical College, East Africa and Aga Khan University Hospital, Nairobi in collaboration with the Ministry of Health brought together national and international experts to promote and strengthen One Health governance for Antimicrobial Resistance (AMR) surveillance in Kenya and the region.

The Conference aims to fill critical gaps in the surveillance of antimicrobial-resistant bacteria in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs), particularly in Sub-Saharan Africa, through various initiatives such as capacity building, research, and surveillance system strengthening to tackle AMR effectively.

The conference invited teams of participants from all over Kenya including 16 health care facilities. Each facility team is composed of an interdisciplinary group of a clinicians, pharmacists, laboratory technologists and an infection prevention and control nurses.

According to the Word Health Organisation, (AMR) is one of the top global public health and development threats. In 2019, it is estimated that bacterial AMR was directly responsible for 1.27 million global deaths and contributed to 4.95 million deaths.

In Kenya, there were 8,500 deaths attributable to AMR and 37,300 deaths associated with AMR in 2019. In addition, Kenya has the 177th highest age-standardized mortality rate per 100,000 population associated with AMR across 204 countries.

Speaking during the conference, Prof Gunturu Revathi, Section Head, Clinical Microbiology, Department of Pathology at the Aga Khan University, quoting the Lancet Commission for Diagnostics said, "Appropriate antimicrobial prescribing requires access to proper diagnostics services and approximately 47% of the global population has little to no access to diagnostics. Diagnostics are central and fundamental to quality health care. This notion is under-recognised, leading to underfunding and inadequate resources at all levels. Importantly, recent international efforts to build laboratory capacity have been intensified and numerous international Non-Governmental Organisations (NGOs) are conducting trainings on Anti-Microbial Stewardship."

"As a leader in medical education, AKU faculty realise that AMR is a patient safety issue, and the laboratory and clinic interphase is an essential component of ensuring patient safety," added Prof Gunturu.

Through the Fleming Fund Country Grant, funded by the UK Department of Health and Social Care (DHSC), the Ministry of Health targets the implementation of the national AMR surveillance strategy in Kenya.In addition, it aims to enhance laboratory performance, data quality, biosafety, and biosecurity while promoting clinical engagement with microbiology services. The goal is to develop a quality-assured surveillance system aligned with the World Health Organization's Global AMR Surveillance System (GLASS).

Dr Emmanuel Tanui, National AMR Focal Point, Ministry of Health said, "The Ministry of Health, through the Antimicrobial Stewardship programs, has deployed a multifaceted approach to address AMR using three pillars which include access, stewardship, research &development. Antimicrobial stewardship programs should strike a balance between the three pillars especially in the Low-and Middle-Income Countries. The stewardship programs ensure access to antimicrobials is not compromised and is expanded where needed."

"The goals of antimicrobial stewardship programs at the Ministry of Health includes, improve safety, quality of care and outcomes, reduce treatment costs, reduce emergence and spread of AMR and optimize antibiotics lifespan," added Dr Tanui.

The Microbiology Conference aims to combat AMR by bringing all the collaborating partners together for networking, actively interacting, enhancing surveillance, strengthening governance, and promoting rational antimicrobial use thereby mitigating the human and economic burden of AMR regionally and globally.
